controlledObservation.text: Morning walkthrough of the warehouse shipping area. The storage mezzanine above the packing benches was being restocked. On the west side there is a pallet-loading opening about twelve feet wide where the forklift lifts pallets up to the deck. The chain that normally goes across that opening was unhooked and lying on the deck, so the edge was open. One of the stockers was working maybe three feet from that open edge with his back to it, moving cartons off a pallet. It is about a ten foot drop to the concrete below. Nobody working up there had a harness on and I did not see any anchor points. The supervisor told me the chain gets unhooked whenever they are loading and they hook it back afterwards. I do not know whether that opening is supposed to have a proper gate or whether the chain is all they have ever had there. Nobody was injured and the forklift was not lifting at the time I was there.
controlledObservation.provenance: Authored fresh for §298. NOT a historical acceptance fixture, NOT a known failure trap, NOT an adversarial puzzle, NOT a driver-role limitation case, NOT malformed, and NOT customer data. No fixture text was copied; the §230 corpus was checked and no case in it is this scenario.
controlledObservation.whyThisOne: An ordinary walkthrough note of the kind an inspector types: one consequential and uncontroversial hazard, one genuine unknown the inspector states in their own words, and two details (nobody injured, the forklift not lifting) that invite over-reading. semanticReview.scope: ONE production observation. NOTHING HERE IS A POPULATION-LEVEL ACCURACY CLAIM and no architectural conclusion is drawn from it.
semanticReview.understoodTheObservation: YES. Ten-foot drop, twelve-foot opening, chain unhooked and on the deck, a stocker three feet from the edge with his back to it, no harness and no anchor points.
semanticReview.identifiedTheConsequentialHazard: YES, and it is the material result of the section. Expert raised the active fall exposure AND recorded a HIGH-confidence disagreement with the deterministic engine, which had marked employee access or exposure CONTRADICTED and suppressed 29 CFR 1910.28 at confidence 0.05. Expert quoted the observation back verbatim to show the exclusion rested on a misreading. That deterministic defect is real, is reproduced below, and is registered as HZ-4.
semanticReview.avoidedManufacturingUnsupportedHazards: YES. Two candidates, both with exact quotes. It did NOT raise a suspended-load hazard and did NOT raise a powered-industrial-truck hazard — both of which the DETERMINISTIC decomposition did raise, the first at Critical with imminentDanger true, on an observation that states the forklift was not lifting.
semanticReview.preservedMaterialUnresolvedFacts: YES. One declaration, decl-gate-requirement, with branchA, branchB, decisionIfA, decisionIfB, decisionWhileUnresolved, whyNecessaryNow and an evidence span quoted from the inspector's own sentence. The declared property is the proposition whose truth controls the corrective action — procedural fix versus facility modification.

humanConfirmation.howThatWasEstablished: The SHIPPED deriveConfirmationRequired was re-run against the STORED posture and returned the same answer the server recorded. Two counterfactuals were run to prove the rule had a real opportunity to fire: with the SAME driver roles but a posture that PERMITS work, confirmation becomes REQUIRED via branch B; and with the declaration's role changed to UNRESOLVED_PROPERTY_CONTROLLING_CONTINUATION, it becomes REQUIRED via branch A.
humanConfirmation.whyItDidNotFire: The posture carries driverRole UNRESOLVED_RESPONSE_OR_FOLLOW_UP, which is branch B's trigger, but branch B additionally requires the posture to permit continued work. The posture is STOP, which does not. Branch A's role is absent. So the answer is a decision, not a vacuous pass.
